result: IFT trains carry FMG1-B as cargo, with beads coated with anti-FMG1-B antibody colocalizing with IFT trains during processive runs (correlation >0.99, p=7×10⁻⁹). The interaction is transient, with FMG1-B boarding and unloading from moving trains.
evaluation: Claims C12 and C13 provide strong quantitative evidence for colocalization (correlation >0.99, statistically significant p-value), while C52 and C53 describe the cargo relationship and transient nature. The multicolor tracking experiments and statistical analysis provide robust support for this result.

result: Pausing of retrograde IFT trains is required for initiation of gliding motility. All paused trains that initiated gliding were retrograde (N=148), with a lag time of 0.48±0.05 s, significantly shorter than the 8.25±0.96 s interval between pausing events (p<0.0001). Anterograde pausing does not initiate gliding.
evaluation: Claims C14-C18 provide converging evidence with appropriate sample sizes (N=148 for directionality, statistical test with p<0.0001). The temporal correlation analysis (C16-C18) and directional specificity (C15, C20) strongly support the conclusion. C21 adds that single trains can be sufficient in 24% of cases.

result: Dynein-1b is the primary motor for gliding motility. Uniflagellate pf18 cells glide at 1.49±0.10 µm/s with flagellum leading. Dynein-1b inactivation (genetic or pharmacological) reduces gliding speed and frequency by 79-92%, while kinesin-2 inactivation increases gliding speed twofold, indicating kinesin-2 plays an inhibitory role.
evaluation: Multiple independent lines of evidence support this result: uniflagellate cell behavior (C22-C25), biflagellate temperature-sensitive mutants (C26-C27), kinesin-2 mutants (C28-C29), and ciliobrevin D inhibition (C30-C32). The convergence of genetic and pharmacological approaches with consistent quantitative measurements provides strong support.

result: IFT-FMG coupling is Ca²⁺-dependent. At normal Ca²⁺ (0.34 mM), 95% of cells display gliding and frequent IFT pausing. At <1 µM Ca²⁺, both gliding and pausing frequency are reduced ~10-fold. Ca²⁺ is required for FMG1-B attachment to IFT trains, not motor activation.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35 provide quantitative dose-response data showing Ca²⁺-dependence of both gliding and pausing. C36, C60-C62 provide mechanistic interpretation supported by the observation that IFT continues normally without Ca²⁺ while beads don't move processively. The inference that Ca²⁺ affects cargo attachment rather than motor activity is well-supported by the data.

result: IFT trains exert 21.4±0.7 pN (anterograde) and 25.2±1.3 pN (retrograde) peak forces as measured by optical trapping. IFT trains remain colocalized with trapped beads with 280±10 nm offset. 20% of retrograde runs escape the trap (>80 pN), while <1% of anterograde runs escape.
evaluation: Claims C37-C42 describe optical trapping measurements with appropriate error estimates and sample sizes (N=11 for offset measurements). The simultaneous TIRF imaging and trapping (C37) validates that forces measured correspond to IFT trains. The asymmetry in escape events (C41-C42) is consistent with the proposed mechanism.

result: Each IFT train is transported by at least four motors, with only one motor type active at a time. Heat-inactivation of kinesin-2 or dynein-1b reduces frequency of respective directional transport but does not alter peak forces in the opposite direction, excluding a tug-of-war mechanism.
evaluation: Claim C5 estimates motor number from force measurements (20-30 pN) divided by single motor stall force (6-7 pN), yielding ~4 motors. Claims C47-C49 provide experimental evidence against tug-of-war through temperature-sensitive mutants. C50 synthesizes these observations into the coordinated transport model. The logic is sound and supported by data.

result: Viscous drag of the membrane slows IFT trains carrying FMG1-B-conjugated beads. Gliding motility (1.49±0.10 µm/s) is slower than retrograde IFT (2.96±0.14 µm/s). IFT trains carrying 1-µm beads move ~30% slower (p<10⁻⁹). The drag constant is 8.0±2.8 pN·s/µm, producing 16-24 pN resistive forces at 2-3 µm/s.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 provide direct speed measurements with statistical significance. C45 measures drag constant from bead recoil experiments. C46 calculates expected resistive forces from drag and velocity, showing they match measured motor forces. C57 synthesizes these into a coherent explanation for speed differences. The quantitative agreement supports the model.

result: During gliding motility, IFT trains pause through surface adhesion of FMG cargos, and dynein-1b motors pull the cell toward the distal tip. Gliding motility in C. reinhardtii is powered by intracellular transport machinery along microtubules, distinct from actin-based or axonemal beating motility.
evaluation: These claims synthesize the major findings into a mechanistic model. C3-C4 describe the mechanism supported by pausing observations (C14-C21) and dynein-1b requirement (C22-C32). C54-C55 place this in broader context. The model is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence.

result: During 60% of gliding reversals (N=40), cells lift one flagellum and paused IFT trains on the surface-adhered flagellum drive motility.
evaluation: Claim C33 provides a specific quantitative observation with adequate sample size (N=40 reversals). This describes one mechanism for directional control during gliding. The observation is straightforward and well-documented.

result: IFT is universal for nearly all eukaryotic cilia and flagella, required for assembly and maintenance. Defects in IFT are linked to polycystic kidney disease, retinal degeneration, and Bardet-Biedl syndrome.
evaluation: These are well-established facts in the field supported by extensive prior literature (multiple citations provided). Claims C1, C7, and C8 provide background context rather than novel findings from this study.

result: IFT trains make multiple connections with the flagellar membrane and carry several ciliary and flagellar membrane proteins. Inactivation of kinesin-2 in fla10ts mutant stops both IFT and gliding motility.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 cite prior work to establish background knowledge. These are not novel findings from this manuscript but provide important context for interpreting the current results.

result: Anterograde IFT trains display rare pauses at approximately 0.02 s⁻¹ per cell (N=27).
evaluation: Claim C19 provides a quantitative measurement with sample size. This observation contrasts with retrograde pausing and supports the directional specificity of the gliding mechanism. The measurement appears straightforward.

result: Kinesin-2 on paused anterograde trains slows down gliding motility by exerting forces in the opposite direction to dynein-1b on paused retrograde trains.
evaluation: Claim C51 proposes a mechanism to explain why kinesin-2 inactivation increases gliding speed (C28-C29). This is consistent with the coordinated transport model (C50) and the observation that only one motor type is active at a time. The proposal is logical given the experimental observations.

result: FMG1-B performs an analogous function to integrins in mammalian cell motility by providing surface adhesion points.
evaluation: Claim C56 draws an analogy between FMG1-B and integrins based on their adhesion functions. This is a reasonable conceptual comparison supported by the demonstrated role of FMG1-B in surface adhesion, though it remains an analogy rather than a mechanistic claim.

result: IFT is unaffected by changes in environmental Ca²⁺ concentration, whereas gliding motility is Ca²⁺-dependent.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 cite prior work and are confirmed by experiments in this study (C34-C36, C60-C61). The distinction between IFT and gliding Ca²⁺-dependence is important for understanding the mechanism.

result: Surface adhesion or crosslinking of FMG1-B induces dephosphorylation of a co-immunoprecipitating transmembrane protein. The complex may be regulated by calcium-calmodulin dependent gliding associated kinase (GAK).
evaluation: Claims C63-C64 cite prior work to provide context for potential signaling mechanisms. These are not findings from this manuscript but relevant background for understanding Ca²⁺-dependent regulation.

result: In a previous trapping assay, beads nonspecifically adsorbed to the flagellar membrane exerted 60 pN average peak forces.
evaluation: Claim C65 cites prior work for comparison with current measurements (20-30 pN). The authors note their lower forces may reflect specific FMG1-B-IFT linkages versus nonspecific adhesion. This provides important context for interpreting force measurements.

result: IFT is required for signal transduction during mating of ciliated organisms. IFT trains transport sexual agglutinins, and adhesion between agglutinins may stall retrograde IFT movement. Microspheres accumulate at flagellar tips during mating.
evaluation: Claim C66 states established knowledge. C67 cites prior work on agglutinin transport. C68 proposes a speculative mechanism for flagellar alignment during mating based on the findings of this study. C69 cites an observation from prior work. The proposed mechanism (C68) is plausible but remains speculative without direct experimental validation.

result: Cilia in retina, liver, and kidney cells make direct physical contacts mediated by N-linked glycoproteins. IFT may exert force on cell-cell adhesion sites and determine their positioning. Ca²⁺ signaling at adhesion sites may regulate attachment to IFT trains and control force generation direction.
evaluation: Claims C70-C71 cite recent work on ciliary contacts. C72-C73 propose speculative extensions of the current findings to other biological contexts. While these proposals are reasonable extrapolations, they lack direct experimental support in this manuscript and remain hypothetical.
